sealed_thresholds.note: registered BEFORE measurement; never tuned to results (Art. XXVII)
sealed_thresholds.ensemble: NONE (single-attacker calibration only; majority-vote ensembles are deferred by the R412 directive)

escalation.reason: measured FPR 1.0 > sealed bar 0.3 (Art. L: the attacker is measured non-selective; its KILL is inadmissible as a terminal verdict and is escalated with the objection preserved)
escalation.rule: the instrument's KILL is measured non-selective (FPR above the sealed bar); the objection is preserved verbatim and ESCALATED for adjudication — the candidate is NOT killed by this attack alone (Art. L); the deterministic gates are unchanged

preserved_objections.basis: The proposed "bias correction layer" that injects diversity by sampling from long-tail items with probability proportional to their inverse popularity directly contradicts fundamental collaborative filtering principles, as evidenced by [doi:10.3850/978-981-07-3043-7_090], which demonstrates that collaborative filtering's strength comes from leveraging actual user preferences, not artificially manipulating recommendation probabilities.

The candidate completely fails to define boundary conditions under which this mechanism would fail or succeed, making it impossible to determine when to apply the correction or how aggressive it should be, leaving the system vulnerable to unpredictable behavior when user preferences shift or content popularity changes.

The candidate cites [doi:10.1145/3308560.3317303] which explicitly states that debiasing feedback loops requires understanding the root causes of bias, not just artificially injecting diversity, directly contradicting the proposed simplistic approach of sampling from long-tail items with inverse popularity probability.

The proposed intervention cannot outperform the baseline because it fails to address the core issue of training on past outputs; instead, it merely adds another layer of artificial manipulation that will eventually become part of the training data itself, creating a new feedback loop that suffers from the same collapsing diversity problem.

The proposed mechanism cannot be implemented because it requires defining "long-tail items" and "inverse popularity" in a dynamic system where these definitions change constantly, making it impossible to establish a stable implementation that doesn't require constant redefinition of parameters.

The testable prediction fails to define what constitutes a "mid-tail user" or how retention will be measured, making it impossible to determine if any observed effects are due to the intervention or other confounding variables, as evidenced by [doi:10.1109/icecet65726.2026.11632531] which shows that measurement ambiguity can lead to false conclusions about system performance.
